cases.abstract: FlashAttention removes quadratic attention intermediates from GPU memory, but avoiding those transfers does not by itself fully exploit the device. FlashAttention-2 addresses the remaining costs of non-matrix arithmetic, limited parallelism, and communication within thread blocks while retaining exact attention. It accumulates unnormalized softmax outputs and normalizes them once, distributes sequence blocks across multiprocessors, and assigns separate query rows to warps so that forward outputs require no inter-warp reduction. These changes preserve quadratic arithmetic complexity while requiring only linear auxiliary storage in sequence length. On an A100 80GB GPU, attention benchmarks spanning sequence lengths from 512 to 16k report 1.7-3.0-fold speedups over FlashAttention and up to 230 TFLOPs/s. The benefit also reaches complete training: GPT-style models with 1.3B or 2.7B parameters on eight A100 GPUs attain up to 1.3-fold higher throughput than with FlashAttention. Gains are larger at 8k than at 2k context. The results establish improved execution of the same attention computation, with application-level benefits that depend on workload rather than matching the largest kernel-level speedup.
cases.methods: FlashAttention-2 computes attention a tile at a time while keeping a running row maximum, an exponential sum, and an unnormalized weighted sum of values. When a new tile changes the maximum, the previous sum and accumulator are rescaled to the new reference; division by the accumulated exponential sum occurs only after all key tiles have been processed. This preserves the softmax result while removing repeated normalization work, which is relatively expensive beside GPU matrix multiplication. Independent query tiles become separate thread blocks, exposing parallelism even when the batch and head counts are small. Within a block, warps own distinct query rows and share keys and values, eliminating the forward reduction required by splitting keys across warps. The backward pass reconstructs probabilities from saved row-wise log-sum-exp statistics. Tile sizes remain constrained: larger tiles can reduce transfers but cause register spilling or exceed shared-memory capacity.
cases.results: The clearest end-to-end contrast is between short and long contexts. For the 1.3B-parameter GPT-style model trained on eight A100 80GB GPUs, FlashAttention-2 raises reported throughput from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 2k context, but from 170 to 220 at 8k. The 2.7B model shows the same pattern: 189 to 205 at 2k and 175 to 225 at 8k. Thus the larger attention-kernel gains translate into roughly 1.3-fold training speedups at 8k, while improvements at 2k remain modest. These throughput figures use the paper's conventional model-FLOP formula, which does not halve attention FLOPs for causal masking. Separately, attention-only benchmarks hold the total token count at 16k as sequence length grows; FlashAttention-2 continues to run at 16k sequence length where standard PyTorch attention runs out of memory. Together, the comparisons support better utilization and practical long-context execution, but they do not make kernel speedup interchangeable with full-model training speedup.
cases.notes: The 230 TFLOPs/s figure is the reported kernel maximum, not the combined forward/backward or end-to-end throughput. Training comparisons use Table 1 and its stated FLOP convention. Exact attention refers to the mathematical operation, not bitwise equality. Prospective H100-specific optimizations are not presented as achieved results.

cases.abstract: Autoregressive generation repeatedly invokes a large model for one token, even when hardware can evaluate several continuations concurrently. Speculative decoding converts that spare concurrency into lower generation latency without changing the target model's output distribution. A smaller model proposes a short continuation, and the target evaluates the associated prefixes in parallel. An acceptance rule based on target and proposal probabilities retains a valid prefix; sampling from a residual distribution corrects the first rejection, while full acceptance permits an additional target token. Distributional correctness holds for any proposal model, whereas acceleration depends on its computational cost and agreement with the target. Under an independent, identically distributed acceptance approximation and unchanged target latency under parallel evaluation, the analysis predicts speedup from draft cost, acceptance, and proposal length. With existing T5 checkpoints, batch size one, and a single TPU-v4, a 77M-parameter draft accelerates T5-XXL generation by 3.4-fold for greedy translation and 2.6-fold for standard sampling; summarization improves by 3.1-fold and 2.3-fold, respectively. Larger drafts accept more proposals but can be slower overall. The method trades increased arithmetic and concurrency for fewer serial target-model steps, rather than reducing inference computation.
cases.methods: Speculative decoding first converts the chosen sampling rule into target and draft distributions p and q. A token drawn from q is accepted with probability min(1,p(x)/q(x)); rejection triggers sampling from the normalized positive part of p-q. The acceptance and correction probabilities together recover p, so the correction preserves the target distribution rather than merely choosing plausible text. The draft proposes gamma tokens sequentially, and the target evaluates gamma+1 prefixes in parallel. The algorithm retains proposals only until the first rejection and then emits one corrected token, or one extra target token after full acceptance. For mean acceptance alpha, expected progress is (1-alpha^(gamma+1))/(1-alpha) tokens per iteration. Dividing this by 1+gamma*c predicts speedup, where c is the draft-to-target per-token runtime ratio. This analysis assumes independent, identically distributed acceptance rates, sufficiently long generations, and no latency increase for parallel target evaluation.
cases.results: The translation experiments show why draft agreement alone is not enough to select a model. With greedy sampling and seven proposals per iteration, T5-large reaches a mean acceptance rate of 0.82 but yields a 1.7-fold speedup, whereas T5-small accepts less, at 0.75, yet reaches 3.4-fold. Both accelerate the same 11B-parameter T5-XXL target at batch size one on a single TPU-v4. The smaller draft therefore offers a better cost-acceptance balance in this setting, despite weaker agreement. Sampling also matters: T5-small achieves 2.6-fold speedup for translation and 2.3-fold for summarization at temperature one, compared with 3.4-fold and 3.1-fold under greedy decoding. These are walltime gains, not arithmetic savings; rejected continuations waste target computation, and acceleration requires available concurrency. Measurements for GPT-like and LaMDA models establish acceptance rates only, so they indicate potential suitability rather than demonstrated latency improvements for those models.
cases.notes: Distributional equivalence is a sampling guarantee, not a claim that individual generated sequences match. Latency evidence is restricted to T5 on one TPU-v4 at batch size one; LaMDA and GPT-like results concern acceptance only. The speedup expression retains the independent, identically distributed approximation and idealized parallel timing. Adaptive proposal counts, beam search, and non-text applications were not validated here.
